noticias.texto:
Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.
At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.
Weekend roundup
- UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.
- Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.
- Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.
- UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
- Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.
In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’
Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).
Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.
But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).
Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”
The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?
Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.
There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.
The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.
And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?
In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.
Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.
It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?
I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?
The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”
But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?
The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.
There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.
Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
The week to come
- Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.
- Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
- Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.
What else we’ve been reading
- With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
- Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy
- Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy
Sport
Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.
Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.
Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield
The front pages
“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.
The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.
The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
Today in Focus
Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?
This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.
Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.
Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

noticias.titulo: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
noticias.resumen: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal. Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.
The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.
According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.
The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.
The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.
At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.
After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.
It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.
However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.
Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.
In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.
The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.
The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.
They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.
The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.
A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”
An embrace of big tech
In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.
The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.
It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.
An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”
The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.
The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.
This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.
As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.
A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.
This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.
The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.
The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.
‘The plan was to migrate everything’
The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.
Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.
The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”
A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.
The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.
Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.
A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.
As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.
Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.
In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.
The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.
Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

noticias.texto:
Burnham sets 3 tests for EU deal, saying it should make Brexit 'closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016'
When Andy Burnham told the Labour conference that he wanted to start a debate on a new relationship with the EU, because Brexit had done more harm than good, he raised the possibility that this could lead to Labour proposing to rejoin at some point after the next election.
But some ministers and Labour MPs are deeply unhappy about that prospect, believing that there would have to be a referendum and that this would be deeply divisive, and there are some signs that Burnham (who is on record as saying he would like the UK to rejoin in his lifetime) is starting to scale back his ambitions.
In his speech to the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham repeated the argument he made in September about Brexit having done more harm than good. But he focused on making Brexit better, not overturning it. At one point in the speech he said:
I don’t believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain. I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years.
And actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016.
And later he said:
People’s jobs depend on working together and collaborating.
And that’s our approach, and it will always be our approach. People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are.
And yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time, respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result.
The reference to “respecting the referendum result” could have just meant not rejoining before the next election. But given that this was a manifesto red line, and that he had already spoken about respecting that, he seemed to imply something more.
And today Burnham has announced three tests for his Brexit reset. (See 9.15am.) Although these are only tests for the deal he is announcing on Friday, not for the Brexit policy he will announce at the next election, the focus on improving the Brexit deal and bringing it “closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016” might be a sign of where his thinking is heading.
In interviews this morning, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, also focused on the government wanting to make Brexit work better for the economy. He told Sky News:
Look, here’s my starting point. My constituents, people across the country, voted for a range of reasons for Brexit, but one of them was one of the biggest, certainly for my constituents, was to make our economy better, positive economic change. We haven’t had that. The economy has got worse. And nobody really thinks this Brexit deal is a good deal.
On ITV’s Good Morning Britain, Ed Balls did not ask Miliband about Russell Brand but he did ask him repeatedly if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU. (See 9.15am.) Miliband and Balls worked very closely together for many years and Balls was clearly assuming that the honest answer would be “Yes”. But Miliband said that he would not give his own personal view because he was abiding by collective cabinet responsibility. Balls said that Andy Burnham has been happy to say he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime, while John Healey (who is 10 years older) has said that he does not expect that in his lifetime. Balls asked Miliband what he expected to happen in his lifetime. Miliband still refused to answer. Balls urged him to be braver and less restrained – “Let your hair down, have a good time” - but Miliband still would not engage with the question.
Badenoch suggests having staggered age of consent would not be practical
Following the Russell Brand conviction, and the revelations about David Walliams, there have been calls for the government to introduce a “staggered” age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds. In an interview yesterday Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said the government would look at this idea.
In her press conference this morning, Kemi Badenoch said that, while she could see the case for this, she did not think it was very practical.
As Sky News reports, she said:
When I was 16, I remember reading the Peter Stringfellow case, a 55-year-old man dating a 16-year-old, and I thought it was the most disgusting thing ever.
I do think ... that there’s some common sense there in terms of a staggered age of consent. My issue is with how we will enforce it.
Badenoch also suggested it would be odd for the government to be raising the age of consent in some circumstances while also lowering the voting age to 16. She went on:
Politicians need to focus on building capacity, building prison spaces, renting spaces abroad, which is one of our policies, rather than creating more laws that cannot be enforced …
[The government is] all over the place. Let’s have an age of maturity and stick to it, and let’s have some coherence in policy.

Tories pledge to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework to limit AI use
The Tories have pledged to halt “screen-based” exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren if the party returns to power, the Press Association reports. PA says:
New guidelines for teachers would seek to ensure that laptops and tablets are not the default in classrooms, the party said.
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said Britain had “sleepwalked into a situation where nearly a million children spend almost every lesson” on a device despite health professionals warning of the dangers of excessive screen time.
Under Conservative proposals, the amount of coursework in school assessment will be “minimised” to make sure the next generation of workers are “AI-resilient”, the party said.
“Screen-based” exams would also be stopped, with screen time for secondary school pupils limited to a maximum of two hours a day, including during homework.
In primary schools, devices would only be used at a “minimum” and where relevant in the curriculum, such as for computing, the party has said.
Kemi Badenoch and Trott will be speaking about this at their press conference starting shortly.
Miliband says he won't resign if Rosebank oilfield approved, despite calling it 'climate vandalism' in 2023
Ed Miliband has said he will not resign from the cabinet if the government approves the Rosebank oilfield, despite his previous condemnation of the scheme.
In an interview on the Today programme, it was put to Miliband that it would be logical for him to resign given that he is on record as saying in 2023 that Rosebank would be “climate vandalism” and a colossal waste of taxpayers’ money.
Asked if he would resign if Labour approves the project, Miliband replied: “No. Definitely not.”
He went on:
I obey collective responsibility. Miatta Fahnbulleh [the energy secretary] will make the decision on this. I know it’s a quasi-judicial decision. So she looks at all the evidence, and then reaches a conclusion. I’m not going to second-guess [her].
Miliband said he supported the decision she made to allow the Jackdaw gasfield to go ahead.
Pressed again on Rosebank, he would not say whether he had changed his mind since he condemned the proposal in 2023. But he said: “I’m a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this.”
As Ben Quinn reports, around 75 Labour MPs have already signed a private letter saying they are opposed to Rosebank going ahead and it is thought that number could rise to more than 100.
Ed Miliband defends doing 2015 election interview with Russell Brand, saying he was ‘taking him on’ not endorsing him
Good morning. There are two issues that will dominate the political news this week – the EU reset, and the Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment – and this morning there are new lines on both of these issues.
Andy Burnham has set out “three tests” for the deal that he is due to agree with the EU at a summit on Friday. Tonight he is giving the traditional prime ministerial speech to the lord mayor’s banquet in London, which by convention focuses on foreign policy, and, according to the overnight briefing from Downing Street, he will announce three tests. No 10 says:
Ahead of this week’s UK-EU Summit, the prime minister will set out three tests for any agreement:
-First, it must be consistent with the manifesto and the government’s red lines.
-Second, it must improve the Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016, rather than the hard Brexit that no one ever seriously argued for in the referendum.
-Third, it must pass the Makerfield test by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives, particularly in communities that have felt neglected for too long.
That means cutting costs for businesses, easing pressure on prices for consumers and creating more opportunities for young people.
If the agreement delivers against these tests, the prime minister will sign it, demonstrating a new approach based on cooperation rather than confrontation.
There is no real doubt about whether the Friday agreement – which will largely focus on food export rules, but which will also cover energy policy (emissions trading rules) and a youth mobility scheme – will pass these tests. Much of it was already agreed when Keir Starmer was PM, and it is more or less a done deal. But Burnham’s “three tests” are interesting because they provide some clues as to how he will approach his plan to have a wider debate about a closer relationship with the EU.
In his speech, Burnham will also restate his view that Brexit has not worked – using a new simile. He will say:
It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the Emperor has nothing on. The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.
Charlie Moloney has more on the Burnham speech here.
Alan Milburn is expected to say that employer national insurance for workers under the age of 25 should be cut in his report published tomorrow, the BBC is reporting.Many of Milburn’s recommendations have already been made public, but this is new, and it is likely to be welcomed by Kemi Badenoch, who is holding a press conference later, because the Tories have repeatedly been saying that Rachel Reeves’s decision to raise employer national insurance has been bad for jobs.
As Alexandra Topping reports, in an article for the Guardian, Burnham has pledged in a Guardian article to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment.
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has been giving interviews this morning. It is relatively unusual for Miliband to be put up for a full interview round and, on Europe and the Milburn report, his remarks were not especially newsworthy. But, on the Today programme, Nick Robinson did get a good line out of him when he asked him about Russell Brand, and Miliband’s decision to do a high-profile interview with Brand during the 2015 election campaign – when Brand had not yet been accused of rape, but when he was already widely viewed as disreputable.
Last week Ed Balls, who was shadow chancellor at the time, twisted the knife by telling his podcast that he had warned Miliband not to go ahead with the “ridiculous” interview. Balls is now a presenter on Good Morning Britain and this morning he was interviewing his old boss and colleague. Sadly, though, he did not ask about Brand.
On the Today programme, when Robinson asked about Balls’s comments last week and put it to Miliband that in 2015 he should have listened to his shadow chancellor, Miliband replied:
Let me first say, Russell Brand’s crimes are heinous and appalling, and all of my sympathies are with the victims of Russell Brand, who have shown incredible bravery.
On the question of that interview, I’ve said … that if I had known of these allegations against Russell Brand, the allegations which he’s now being convicted [of], I would never have done that interview, and I deeply regret it.
Miliband claimed that he did not know at the time about Balls’s reservations about the interview going ahead, but he said Balls was “obviously right” about Brand being weird and untrustworthy.
But Miliband went on to defend doing the interview. He said:
Let me just say one thing, because I do want to one thing you said.
Russell Brand was going around telling people not to vote in the general election.
I was not endorsing Russell Brand. I was taking him on and saying he was completely wrong in saying that people shouldn’t vote, that democracy didn’t matter and all those things. But as I say, I deeply regret doing that interview.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: Kemi Badenoch and Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hold a press conference.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

noticias.titulo: Man charged after two people die in Leeds police pursuit crash
noticias.resumen: Leigh Ross, 39, charged with causing death by dangerous driving after BMW being pursued by police collided with another car A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving after two people were killed when their car was hit by a vehicle being chased by police. A 22-year-old man and 23-year-old woman, both from York, died when their car was struck by a BMW being pursued by police in Leeds in the early hours of Sunday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving after two people were killed when their car was hit by a vehicle being chased by police.
A 22-year-old man and 23-year-old woman, both from York, died when their car was struck by a BMW being pursued by police in Leeds in the early hours of Sunday.
Leigh Ross, 39, will appear in court on Monday charged with causing death by dangerous driving and other offences.
West Yorkshire police said Ross, from Harrogate, had been charged with two counts of causing death by driving a vehicle while unlicensed or uninsured, failing to stop a mechanically propelled vehicle when required by a constable, and aggravated vehicle taking.
Two boys, aged 16 and 17, and a 16-year-old girl, who were also arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, have been released on bail pending further inquiries, the force said.
West Yorkshire police have referred themselves to the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which has launched an investigation into the incident.
The crash happened shortly after a blue BMW 123d allegedly failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco.
The driver, a 22-year-old man, was pronounced dead at the scene while his passenger, a 23-year-old woman, died later in hospital. Specialist family liaison officers are supporting their families, who have asked for privacy.
Detectives are appealing for any witnesses who saw the collision, or have dashcam, mobile phone or CCTV footage, to contact West Yorkshire police via 101 or online.

noticias.titulo: Boots to begin prescribing medical cannabis in UK
noticias.resumen: Online service will be offered to patients with eligible conditions, in a first for a British high street pharmacy Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy. The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy.
The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia.
The chain is launching its SureLeaf service alongside a collaborative research programme with the University of Nottingham that will examine patient outcomes, prescribing practices and experience in the treatment of chronic pain.
Patients will be invited to start an assessment online. Their suitability will then be reviewed by a clinical team, before they are invited to a video consultation with a consultant, according to Boots.
Boots said any prescription would be “independently reviewed by a multidisciplinary clinical team that includes a second, independent consultant, before treatment begins”. It said any patient wishing to be prescribed medical cannabis must first have tried conventional treatments without success. And the pharmacy said patients would be regularly reviewed.
Boots’ chief healthcare officer, Jamie Kerruish, said: “Millions of people live with ongoing pain and, for some, conventional treatments do not provide adequate symptom relief. This can have a significant impact on everyday life, from working and sleeping well to spending time with family and doing the things they enjoy.
“Ultimately, it’s about helping people explore appropriate options that could help them better manage their symptoms and improve their quality of life.”
Dr David Gwynne, the medical director of Boots’ online service, said: “Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone and prescribing decisions need to be made carefully on an individual patient basis.
“SureLeaf has, therefore, been designed with strong clinical safeguards and specialist oversight at every stage, so treatment is only considered for patients where it is clinically appropriate. Our priority is to ensure patients receive responsible, clinically led care, from their initial specialist assessment through to ongoing monitoring and review once treatment begins.”
The prescription of cannabis-derived medicines was legalised in 2018 after the mother of a young boy from Northern Ireland with severe epilepsy had cannabis oil seized at airport customs. Many private clinics have been treating patients with them for years.
Hopes have been expressed that cannabis could revolutionise some areas of medicine. Only people with rare forms of epilepsy, those dealing with certain side-effects of chemotherapy, and those with certain multiple sclerosis symptoms, can get it on the NHS. But, besides chronic pain, private clinics have also been prescribing the medicines for various psychiatric disorders and neurological conditions.
This year, researchers from universities in Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne in Australia, and Bath in England, found “very little evidence” that cannabis was effective in treating anxiety, anorexia nervosa, psychotic disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder or opioid use disorder.
They found some evidence the medical products could reduce dependence on cannabis, relieve the symptoms of Tourette syndrome and help insomniacs sleep better.

noticias.texto:
Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial.
Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action.
A series of rape myths were allegedly deployed in the defence of Brand, 51, during his trial at Southwark crown court, including the argument that his accusers should not be believed because they had not screamed, kicked or fled.
Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.
In his closing speech to the jury, Brand’s defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, argued that the comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.
Winter asked the jury whether they could be sure that of the “many, many women” Brand had slept with over a decade, he had “raped just three of them”.
Winter has reported himself to the BSB after criticisms over an exchange with a Sunday Times journalist outside court as well as his conduct within it.
Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: “[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large.”
A spokesperson for the BSB told the Times it agreed that rape and sexual assault cases “must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice”. They added: “That is one of the reasons why we set up an expert reference group to advise on strengthening standards for barristers acting in rape and serious sexual offence cases.”
A spokesperson for the Bar Council, which represents barristers, told the paper that a defendant denying a rape charge had a right to have evidence tested in court, and stressed the importance of the BSB remaining independent of the government.
In a separate development, Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, shared a message from her jailed husband in which he claimed he was “not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening”.
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said Brand’s message was “disgusting” and apologised for appearing on the disgraced comedian’s online show as Labour leader in 2015.
Miliband told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.
“I’ve said that if I’d known any of these allegations against him, I would never have done that interview, and I regret doing it.”
Meanwhile, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, urged the entertainment industry to “get its house in order” or face a government crackdown.
She is due to meet senior media, arts and sports figures on Monday and will call on them to introduce systems to protect young employees and freelancers from harassment and abuse by older, more powerful men.
Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from the category B Wandsworth prison in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

noticias.titulo: DOJ warns Elizabeth Warren over Trump investigations – US politics live
noticias.resumen: Letter to likely chair of Senate Banking Committee is latest warning to Democrats about their potential plans following midterms success Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, was warned by he US Department of ⁠Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into ​president Donald Trump. Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China
noticias.texto:
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, was warned by he US Department of Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into president Donald Trump.
It is the latest warning sent by the justice department to congressional Democrats about their potential plans to investigate the administration or Trump associates, Reuters reported.
Trump last week ordered the department to look into Democratic lawmakers for “threatening” people, and US attorney-general Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that his agency was prepared to battle congressional Democrats.
In a letter to Warren, US attorney Aaron Reitz in Houston told the Massachusetts Democrat she appeared “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of president Trump’s private associates”.
Reitz told her to preserve materials “relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights”.
Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reitz shared the letter on social media and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.
Warren and other Democrats have signaled that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, among others.
In other developments:
Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days.
Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances. Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.
US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but transportation secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normal by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.
After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024. Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.
On CNN’s State of the Union, he reaffirmed that he believes he has a path to victory, citing support and a widespread openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus.
“This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Van Hollen said, alluding to how the US president’s Republican party lost control of Congress during the 3 November midterm elections.
“They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.”

Reitz told her to preserve materials “relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights”.
Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reitz shared the letter on social media and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.
Warren and other Democrats have signaled that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, among others.
In other developments:
Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days.
Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances. Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.
US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but transportation secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normal by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.
After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024. Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

noticias.titulo: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
noticias.resumen: Surge in prices is forcing many to cut back on spending, with a projected 21% increase in costs of those households Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil. The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.
The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases.
About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east.
A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east.
Residents in Maine, where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter.
“My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill”
It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses.
“Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.”
Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil.
“We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.”
Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating.
“We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.”
Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US.
“It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.”
Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living.
Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average.
Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel.
The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far.
Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years.
The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive. Lately, my bills have averaged around $350 a month, which is starting to feel like the new normal,” Carpenter said.
Carpenter said he’s concerned about the effect higher prices will have on the ability of younger generations, including his children, to save for emergencies.
“When necessities take up more of your budget, there’s less left for an unexpected car repair or a roof that needs replacing,” he added. “What concerns me goes beyond energy. It’s the combined cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and other necessities. Inflation means our money doesn’t stretch as far.”

noticias.titulo: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
noticias.resumen: CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, as US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’ Megaspeed says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ Business live – latest updates Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation. An open letter, which has more than 165,000 signatories, demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establis
noticias.texto:
Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.
An open letter, which has more than 165,000 signatories, demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia CEO’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two big shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
In Washington, however, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next CEO. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.
Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing, Alice Huang.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to China – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.
One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”.
Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option.
“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.
US lawmakers have said that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the House select committee on China, as well as the foreign affairs and the intelligence committees. The dates of the appearances, likely to be behind closed doors, have not been confirmed.
On Sunday, Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Haung was an executive until she left in 2025, said it is a “legitimate and lawful business”.
In the past three years, the company was one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.
Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, the president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.
Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.
But the company – which will report on its quarterly earnings on Tuesday – has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

noticias.titulo: Huge waves pummel California coast, forcing closure of popular piers
noticias.resumen: Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers. The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers.
The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.
On Saturday, waves above 50ft were recorded in San Mateo county, just south of San Francisco.
Surfers weren’t deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks beach near Half Moon Bay.
Farther south, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.
In southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego’s Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.
At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, known for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.
Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.
The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

noticias.titulo: South Africa: 17 killed in separate mass shooting incidents
noticias.resumen: Police are investigating two mass shooting incidents in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. There has been a growing trend of mass shooting incidents making headlines in recent years.
noticias.texto:
South Africa: 17 killed in separate mass shooting incidents
November 16, 2026
At least 17 people have been killed in two separate shooting incidents in South Africa, police said on Monday.
South Africa is battling extremely high levels of violent crime with around 60 people killed every day.
What we know about the latest incidents
The South African Police Service (SAPS) said in a statement that nine bodies were found early on Monday in an informal settlement outside of the capital Pretoria in Gauteng province.
A police spokeswoman said that officers were alerted to the scene at 07:30 a.m. (0530 UTC/GMT) and on arrival found six dead males and three dead females inside a shack, all with gunshot wounds.
Police said a motive for the shooting had not yet been established and that no arrests had been made.
In the second incident, police said that a bullet-riddled vehicle was found in a semi-rural area outside the city of Pietermaritzburg in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal.
"Inside the vehicle police found eight men who had multiple gunshot wounds and were certified dead at the scene," a police statement said.
Police said they were also still trying to determine a motive and were working to identify the victims.
"We have seen these kinds of shootings before and there have been different motives from stock theft-related, to drugs-related to taxi violence," KwaZulu-Natal province police spokesman, Colonel Robert Netshiunda, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.
South Africa's high rates of crime
In September, at least 28 people were gunned down in mass shootings in Gauteng and the Western Cape in two of the most recent incidents.
Over the years, South Africa has consistently ranked among the countries with the world's highest murder rates, recording between 36 and 45 murders per 100,000 people annually.
The country also continues to grapple with high levels of gender-based violence, sexual violence and other contact crimes while police battle with large case loads, contributing to low convictions rates.

noticias.titulo: Polish police arrest 3 teens over suspected neo-Nazi terror plot
noticias.resumen: Investigators found information sharing on how to make explosives at home as well as chemicals needed for that purpose.
noticias.texto:
Polish police arrest 3 teens over suspected neo-Nazi terror plot
November 16, 2026
Three teenagers have been arrested in Poland on suspicion of planning a terror attack, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland's special services, said in a post on social media on Monday.
The suspects, a 16-year-old and two 17-year-olds, allegedly had links to an international neo-Nazi movement.
The arrest comes days after a gunman with reported far-right leanings opened fire in Krakow, killing six people.
What do we know about the suspected neo-Nazi terror plot?
Siemoniak said in his post on X that the three teenagers had been arrested by the officials of the Internal Security Agency (ABW).
"The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had already begun taking steps toward committing terrorist offenses," he said.
During a search, ABW agents discovered chemicals used to make explosives, according to the minister.
The suspects were also found to have exchanged information over messaging platforms on how to make explosives, firearms and pyrotechnics at home, with the intended use of carrying out a terror attack.
The two 17-year-olds have been taken into pre-trial detention, with the 16-year-old being sent to a juvenile detention facility, Siemoniak said.
Poland is on high alert after 24-year-old Michal Oksinski killed six people and injured 15 more when he started shooting on Krakow's Main Market Square on November 7.
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said Oksinski had been fascinated with Norwegian neo-Nazi mass killer Anders Breivik and had amassed a large amount of ammunition before his rampage.

noticias.titulo: Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims
noticias.resumen: Jordan has imposed a ban on Telegram over a deadly church attack which left seven people dead. The kingdom claims that content on the messaging app poses a threat to "national interests."
noticias.texto:
Jordan bans Telegram over 'extremism' and 'radicalization' concerns
November 16, 2026
Jordan on Monday announced a ban on instant messaging service Telegram after a deadly attack on a church last month.
Jordan's Public Security Directorate said the move aimed to protect the society from "the attempts to spread extremism and radicalisation."
All of which pose a "threat to societal security and national interests," it said.
In December 2022, Jordan also banned TikTok over videos authorities claimed "promoted killing and chaos."
What prompted the ban?
The ban on Telegram comes after a shooting on October 23 at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak governate which left seven people dead and another 34 wounded.
Jordan, in retaliation, organised airstrikes on neighbouring Syria and said it had killed 20 so-called "Islamic State" militants. The government also acknowledged that a number of civilians had been killed in the strikes.
A Jordanian court sentenced three men to death by hanging on Sunday in connection with the attack. Authorities identified them as "followers of a hardline Islamist ideology."
Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state and close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.
Christians make up around 3% of Jordan's population of 10 million. The Levantine country is home to one of the oldest Christian communities in the world.
Telegram and 'IS'
Over the years, so-called "Islamic State" militants have used Telegram for propaganda and communication purposes.
The Russian-born billionaire Pavel Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013.
In July, Russia said it had charged him with "aiding terrorist activities," accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.
Durov rejects the allegations, arguing that Telegram has gone "beyond its obligations in moderating content and assisting authorities in tackling crime."
He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Merz heads to Munich for talks with CSU
noticias.resumen: Chancellor Friedrich Merz starts the week with his Bavarian allies. Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. And an autobahn "bridge to nowhere" will finally link up to the road network. Follow DW.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Merz heads to Munich for talks with CSU
Published November 16, 2026last updated November 16, 2026
What you need to know
- Friedrich Merz visits Munich for talks with Markus Söder and CSU leadership
- Manuela Schwesig set for vote on another term as state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
- NRW leaders head to ground-breaking ceremony as the A44 autobahn's 'bridge to nowhere' near Düsseldorf will finally be linked up to the network
- German national team gears up for evening Nations League match against neighbors and rivals Netherlands
Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.
Markus Söder: Cutting electricity tax key for 'credibility'
Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.
It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.
Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.
Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."
He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.
"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."
Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."
AfD chocolate Saint Nicholas in party's fan shop upsets religious leaders
A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.
Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.
The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.
"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."
Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.
Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.
The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.
He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."
"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.
All welcome at Bavarian politician Aiwanger's funeral, partner says
The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.
Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.
"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.
She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.
Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.
Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.
Germany's Nations League fate at stake against Netherlands
Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.
And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.
If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.
Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.
"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."
A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.
Work starting to link A44 'bridge to nowhere' to road network
The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.
Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.
A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.
State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.
